summary: The 2023 Nobel Prize in chemistry went to Moungi Bawendi, Louis Brus and Alexei Ekimov for discovering and creating quantum dots, tiny specks whose color and other properties depend on their size. Ekimov and Brus showed in the early 1980s that size and color are linked, and Bawendi later devised a method to grow dots to precise sizes. Quantum dots are now used in TV screens, LED lighting and medical imaging, with potential in solar panels and quantum computers.
one_line: Bawendi, Brus and Ekimov won the 2023 chemistry Nobel for discovering and producing quantum dots, size-tunable nanocrystals used in displays and medicine.
key_facts: The 2023 Nobel Prize in chemistry honors Moungi Bawendi, Louis Brus and Alexei Ekimov for discovering and creating quantum dots.
The trio will split a prize of 11 million Swedish kronor, or about $1 million; the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced it October 4.

Quantum dots are each a few billionths of a meter across, and quantum mechanics governs how their size alters properties such as interaction with light and electricity, magnetism and melting temperature.
Smaller quantum dots give off bluer fluorescent light, while bigger dots give off redder light, without changing the dots' molecules.
In the early 1980s, Alexei Ekimov made quantum dots in glass by adding copper chloride, producing tiny crystals whose size was linked to the glass's color.
Louis Brus independently showed a link between size and color for nanosize particles floating in a solution or in a gas.
About a decade later, Moungi Bawendi devised a method that injected chemicals into a solution to form tiny crystals, then tweaked the temperature to halt growth at a desired size.

Bawendi met Brus and began working on quantum dots at Nokia Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., where researchers needed high-quality dots to study nanoparticle physics; the method took years of trial and error.
Quantum dots can subtly change the color of LED lights, which can dramatically improve their energy efficiency.
Surgeons can attach fluorescent quantum dots to immune cells that swarm cancerous tissues to spot hard-to-see tumors.
Scientists suspected nearly a century ago that nanoparticle size could alter properties, but making such particles seemed impossible.
Warren Chan's group at the University of Toronto used quantum dots to tag cells in the 1990s and is now using them to detect infections such as flu and HIV.
Heiner Linke of the Nobel committee said "Quantum dots are a new class of materials, different from molecules."
